name: Seizure Prediction
title: Seizure Prediction
answer: Seizure prediction is the use of machine learning to estimate the likelihood that a person with epilepsy will have a seizure within a short upcoming window, usually minutes to hours, based on physiological signals. It is distinct from seizure detection, which identifies a seizure as it happens. The work sits within neuroinformatics and clinical AI, drawing on electroencephalography, electrocardiography, accelerometry, and other wearable data. The goal is to give patients and caregivers enough lead time to move to safety, take a prescribed rescue medication, or adjust activity.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Seizure prediction is the use of machine learning to estimate the likelihood that a person with epilepsy will have a seizure within a short upcoming window, usually minutes to hours, based on physiological signals. It is distinct from seizure detection, which identifies a seizure as it happens. The work sits within neuroinformatics and clinical AI, drawing on electroencephalography, electrocardiography, accelerometry, and other wearable data. The goal is to give patients and caregivers enough lead time to move to safety, take a prescribed rescue medication, or adjust activity.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most research and early clinical systems run on continuous or long term EEG recordings, often from implanted or scalp electrodes, combined with wearable sensors for heart rate, motion, and skin conductance. Computation may happen on a bedside unit, a smartphone, or a cloud service, with newer work moving toward on device inference to reduce latency and protect privacy. Training typically requires large, patient specific archives of interictal and preictal segments, which are expensive to collect and label.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The common approach is to turn raw signals into features such as spectral power, connectivity, heart rate variability, or entropy, then train a classifier or sequence model to separate preictal from interictal states. Patient specific models are standard because seizure patterns vary widely between people, and transfer learning or federated approaches are used to borrow strength across patients without pooling raw data. Performance is usually reported with sensitivity, false positive rate per day, and time in warning, and a useful predictor must beat a random or cyclical baseline.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Seizure prediction models are medical devices in most jurisdictions and face regulatory review for safety and effectiveness before clinical use. False alarms can cause anxiety or alarm fatigue, while missed predictions can create a false sense of security, so risk communication and clear labeling of model uncertainty matter. Data provenance is a serious issue because EEG and wearable records are sensitive health data, and consent, deidentification, and secondary use rules apply. Product liability questions are live in medical AI, and this site tracks active lawsuits and compliance pages relevant to such tools.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving from retrospective proof of concept toward prospective, long term home monitoring studies that measure real world false alarm burden and patient benefit. Closed loop systems that pair a seizure predictor with an implanted neurostimulator or drug delivery device are an active research direction, though they raise higher safety and regulatory stakes. More interpretable models and standardized benchmarks may help clinicians trust and compare systems, while patient reported outcomes are becoming part of evaluation rather than accuracy alone.
